sceneHappening: Longing for a heavenly home, the love of Christ that compels, and the ministry of reconciliation
summary: Paul knows that if the earthly tent they live in is destroyed, they have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Meanwhile they groan, longing to be clothed with their heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. God has prepared them for this and has given them the Spirit as a pledge. So they are always confident, knowing that while at home in the body they are away from the Lord, "for we walk by faith, not by sight." They would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Whether at home or away, they aim to please him, "for we must all be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ." Knowing the fear of the Lord, they persuade people. Paul says they are not commending themselves again, but giving the Corinthians cause to be proud on their behalf. "If we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or if we are in our right mind, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus: that one died for all, therefore all died; and he died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again." From now on they regard no one according to the flesh; "if any man is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new." All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation. "We are ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God. For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God."
whySettingMatters: Paul knew tents: he was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), so a body as a "tent" is a natural picture, temporary and easily taken down. What Paul expects between death and resurrection is debated. His language of being "unclothed" (5:3-4) may point to an intermediate state with Christ before the bodily resurrection, or to the exchange of a mortal body for an immortal one at once; he does not spell out the details, and the passage should be read with 1 Corinthians 15. The "judgment seat" (bema) was the raised platform where Roman officials judged, familiar in Corinth, which had one in its forum. In 5:16, "we regard no one according to the flesh" and "even though we have known Christ according to the flesh" are debated; they probably mean judging by outward status, not by the new reality in Christ. "New creation" echoes Isaiah's promise of new heavens and earth (Isaiah 43:18-19; 65:17). The word "reconcile" was used in diplomacy, which fits "ambassadors." "Made him to be sin" is also read as "made him a sin offering" (the Greek word for sin was used for the sin offering in the Old Testament); either way Paul is describing exchange.

people.note: Longs for the heavenly home and describes the ministry of reconciliation.
Died for all, rose again, and was "made sin" on our behalf.

questions: Paul says we "walk by faith, not by sight." What does that look like day to day?
"The love of Christ compels us." How does that explain Paul's choices, even strange ones?
What does "new creation" mean for how we see other people, as Paul says, "no longer according to the flesh"?
Paul calls Christians ambassadors who plead, "be reconciled to God." What does the picture of ambassador say about our role?
